awd_titl_txt: Conference: FASEB Conference on Mechanisms in Plant Development Meeting
awd_abstract_narration:
Plants grow and adapt through complex developmental processes, from root formation underground to leaf and flower development above. Understanding how plants build and shape themselves not only advances science but also helps address real-world challenges in agriculture resilience and efficiency and food security. The 2025 FASEB Conference on Mechanisms in Plant Development will bring together leading scientists and early career researchers to share discoveries about how plants grow and respond to their environments. Taking place in Southbridge, Massachusetts, this meeting is the only recurring international forum fully focused on plant development. This conference ensures shared open discussion of the latest scientific tools, like single-cell technologies and live-cell imaging, so that more researchers can use these new techniques to explore plant systems in greater detail than ever before. The meeting also offers dedicated workshops and networking opportunities for students and early-career researchers to build skills and mentorship relationships, fostering a new generation of plant researchers. These efforts contribute to a highly trained workforce capable of developing innovative solutions for agriculture, while also strengthening the U.S. leadership in plant science and biotechnology.

The 2025 FASEB Conference on Mechanisms in Plant Development will convene a multidisciplinary community of scientists exploring the genetic, molecular, and cellular mechanisms underlying plant development. With rapid advancements in single-cell transcriptomics, super-resolution microscopy, and computational modeling, the field is poised to make transformative discoveries in developmental biology. This meeting will feature sessions on key topics such as morphogenesis, growth control, hormonal signaling, patterning, and root architecture, with an emphasis on how plants establish structure and respond to environmental signals. Scientific sessions will include 32 invited talks and 22 selected presentations from emerging researchers, fostering a comprehensive exchange of unpublished research. Two keynote lectures will honor the groundbreaking contributions of Philip Benfey and Joanne Chory, whose work has significantly shaped the fields of root development and plant hormone signaling. A core focus of the meeting is cross-disciplinary dialogue, bringing together experts in molecular genetics, cell biology, biophysics, and systems biology to explore new conceptual frameworks and methodologies. Professional development workshops will support early-career researchers through targeted training in publishing, grant writing, interdisciplinary research, and mentorship. By combining cutting-edge research with training and networking, this conference will advance the frontiers of plant developmental biology and support the next generation of scientific leaders.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Plants build roots, leaves, flowers, and seeds through coordinated processes that connect genes, cells, and their environment. Understanding these processes advances fundamental biology and provides a foundation for improving crops. This award supported the 2025 FASEB Conference on Mechanisms in Plant Development, held August 24–28, 2025, in Southbridge, Massachusetts, bringing researchers together to share discoveries about how plants grow and develop.

Organized by Ross Sozzani of North Carolina State University with co-organizers Ikram Blilou and Alexis Maizel, the conference connected researchers across disciplines and career stages. Registration records documented 107 registrants, including 25 graduate students, 23 postdoctoral fellows, and 27 early-career faculty members. The final program included two keynote lectures, 22 invited talks, 24 selected talks, and 77 numbered posters.

The scientific program explored how plants establish cell identities, shape organs, repair damaged tissues, and adjust development in response to environmental conditions. Researchers shared approaches that connect molecular biology with imaging, physics, mathematics, and engineering. For example, studies of individual cells examined how specialized tissues develop, while research on cell walls and mechanical forces explored how physical properties influence plant shape. Other contributions investigated genetic circuits for modifying root development and methods for controlling gene activity.

These exchanges helped connect research across biological scales—from events inside individual cells to the formation of entire organs. Comparisons among model plants and crops, including maize, tomato, rice, and barley, provided opportunities to examine shared developmental mechanisms and differences among species. The award’s scientific contribution was to enable presentation and discussion of this research, helping participants encounter methods and ideas relevant to their own work.

Training and professional development were central to the meeting. Selected talks and poster sessions offered opportunities to explain findings, answer questions, and discuss research with other scientists. A dedicated panel, “Career Development in Academia: From Graduate Studies to Tenure Track,” brought together eight established researchers to share perspectives on academic career progression. Meals, breaks, and poster discussions provided additional opportunities for mentoring and professional connections. 

The conference also honored the scientific legacies of Philip Benfey and Joanne Chory through memorial keynote lectures delivered by Siobhan Brady and Niko Geldner.

The award’s immediate outcomes were scientific exchange, interdisciplinary learning, and researcher development. Its potential longer-term benefits include wider use of complementary research methods and a stronger workforce prepared to advance plant science. Knowledge shared about roots, regeneration, plant architecture, and environmental responses may ultimately inform agricultural biotechnology and crop improvement, contributing to efforts to address food security.
